nodes.title: Pivotal: a DSL for data analysis in Python
nodes.body:
I have been working on language for data analysis, has some similarities to IBIS (one syntax multiple backends). Except its a DSL that compiles to Python (pandas, polars, duckdb) intended to be used within Jupyter notebooks:

https://nealhughes.net/pivotal/

https://github.com/nealbob/pivotal-py

Would really welcome any feedback on this. The first link above explains my motivation. (Sorry if this is unwelcome)
This is cool! Can you compare/contrast with [PRQL](https://prql-lang.org/)?

The other real value-adds that I think a next-gen relational-algebra DSL should have:
- type safety, eg renaming a column upstream gives errors when downstream calculations rely on the old name
- serializability, eg being able to define a query with a html builder, then being able to persist this in a DB or push it over the network so the server can execute it
- extensibility, eg when someone wants to support a new backend, they can do that with NO needed support from the core. Otherwise you end up like ibis where I feel really bogged down trying to keep the flink tests passing even though I have never and will never use that not very popular backend.
- excellent developer tooling, eg LSP, autocomplete, etc

If you are interested, these properties are the motivation behind https://github.com/NickCrews/tybis, an experiment in trying to take all the good parts of ibis and make them even better, in typescript.

Hi Nick, thanks for the response. 

Yes, PRQL especially if used in DuckDB / Python is probably closest to Pivotal in spirit. I think the key difference is the audience / use case: I'm targeting analytical work with small /medium in-memory data in Python (this is what I do for work,  I don't really use DBs / SQL much).

I do have a simple comparison of Pivotal and PRQL syntax [here](https://nealhughes.net/pivotal-py/comparison/#__tabbed_1_5) and touched on it briefly in this [post](https://nealhughes.net/pivotal-py/whypivotal/):

> In some respects, DuckDB and PRQL address similar problems as Pivotal, just from the opposite direction: trying to modify SQL to bring it closer to Python, rather than building a native Python workflow that is more SQL like.
>Ultimately, there are limits to how far you can bend SQL to suit Python analytical workflows. In practice, the mental (and performance) overhead of moving data between a SQL engine and Python can slow things down (especially for exploratory work on small datasets).

Syntax wise PRQL is still slightly more verbose than Pivotal (more brackets, aliases in merge etc.). But it gets back to the point above: PRQL is built on SQL and SQL is built for databases. There are lot of things in Python workflows that don’t fit naturally in SQL like, linking operations to metadata, saving results, plotting, functions / loops. Piped SQL / PRQL helps a bit, but why not have something built for in-memory analytical work from the start.

On your other points. 

- I'm interested in type safety but haven't looked into it yet. It reminds me of [Pluto.jl](https://plutojl.org/) reactive notebooks, this idea that MS Excel solved this upstream/downstream dependency thing a long time ago and notebooks have gone backwards in a sense. Seems like you could build a DAG from a pipeline style DSL without too much trouble, and use it for this purpose.
- Serializability may be less relevant for our use case
- I've tried to keep extensibility in mind, but its still Python centric. Longer-term I would like to extend Pivotal beyond Python, with a common core (maybe in Rust) that could be linked to R or Julia
- No LSP yet, but there is auto-complete etc. via VS Code / Jupyter Lab extensions

nodes.title: Discuss: PEP 827 – Type Manipulation
nodes.body:
FRom the abstract of https://peps.python.org/pep-0827/:

> We propose adding powerful type-level introspection and construction facilities to Python’s type system. This design is inspired largely by TypeScript’s conditional and mapped types, but is adapted to the distinct semantics and constraints of Python’s typing model.
> 
> From the bird’s-eye view, this proposal aims to:
> 
> - introduce new primitives in the typing module;
> - broaden the annotation syntax supported by static type checkers, without requiring changes to Python’s grammar;
> - ensure that the new type-level machinery benefits both static type checkers and frameworks that rely on runtime type introspection.

I wanted to make there be a discussion here in ibis, because I think this would really affect how we could type our APIs for users. For example, I think we could then actually track the schema of a table throughout processing, eg so we can error if the user tries to access a column that doesn't exist.

In general I would like such a feature to exist in python's typing. But I haven't read the proposal in much detail, so I don't have specific critiques of it. But if you have thoughts, please chime in here!

Hey Nick thanks for mentioning this pep which I agree is useful for ibis and several other libraries my team uses that involve schema-like classes and operations on those. Assuming others agree wrt ibis, would your thoughts be to check for any gaps in the proposal vs needs in ibis, and vice support in the comments for the pep?

nodes.title: Poll: Opinions on importance of typing
nodes.body:
I have been trying to improve the type annotations of ibis over the last year, because I value the hints my IDE gives me when I'm doing something stupid. But I wanted to get a feel for other's opinions here.

First, I just want to caveat: We don't have any type checker set up, and if we did it would have so many spurious errors it would be useless, so at this point we are judging all the following criteria on a best-effort basis, since we can't enforce any of them with CI.

I think my proposal for an official stance is
- Ibis has a best-effort stance on type annotations. If you use a typechecker with your ibis code, you are going to get errors. We will try to reduce the number of these, but it is not our goal to eliminate type errors entirely.
- All PRs MUST NOT worsen type coverage
- New features MUST have type annotations on all public APIs.
- New features weakly SHOULD (I'm fine weakening this to a COULD if you give pushback) have type annotations on internal APIs when they really would benefit from them.
- Refactors COULD improve type annotations, but no expectation.
- We use [ty](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty) as our official implementation in case of conflicts between type checkers.

Any thoughts on this proposal? Additional stances we could take?

nodes.title: Automatically checking expression backend compatibility
nodes.body:
I recently posted a little blog about automatically checking which backends an expression will work on.

Would love to see if this is way off base or if there's a secret way to do this built into Ibis already.

Blog: https://iwhalen.com/ibis-compatibility/
Repo: https://github.com/iwhalen/ibis-compatibility

Very cool! I'm not personally aware of anything built-in to do this (@NickCrews do you know? :)). From an approach perspective, my first thought was also `has_operation`/doing things in the way of the operation support matrix, but your reasoning and alternative approach makes sense.

My thoughts are:

- It's not ideal that you have to hit the matrix and parse it each time you instantiate the checker. It also makes it dependent on the matrix format (which, to be fair, doesn't really change).
- The bigger drawback in my opinion is that you see the latest support matrix (off `main`) as opposed to that for any version.

I wonder if it would make sense to just run a process that computes the matrix for a tagged release (probably check out the code, install all the dependencies, run the same code but output to a file), store thise matrices on GitHub or wherever, and that way any users just download that file instead of scraping latest?

Thanks for taking a peek @deepyaman! 

I [incorporated](https://github.com/iwhalen/ibis-compatibility/pull/2) your suggestions. 

Once I get the docs building locally I'll remove the piece that parses from the docs site😁(re: #11799)

Thanks, this is cool. I think your solution is probably the best possible at this time, there is no secret backdoor in the internals that I know of. In fact, I've never even looked at the matrix generator code.

I also am curious what you think about the simple true/false for support, for example some backends only support some args to certain operations, eg (this isn't exactly right but you get the idea) you can only exclude nulls in ArrayCollect on sqlite, if you do .collect(include_nulls=True) you get a runtime error. So that in my mind is partial support for the general ArrayCollect op, only with a concrete instance of ArrayCollect would you be able to tell.

Ideas on how ibis could improve here:
- don't require eg psycopg to be installed to compile expressions to postgres, and check for compatibility. You only need psycopg to execute.
-improve how backends declare their support for operations so they can be analyzed statically/declaratively (I actually have no idea how this is currently done but I bet it takes some actual execution)
- when we compute the support matrix, we could save that as a machine readable file eg Json for easier and more stable consumption.
- we could actually publish this in a release for this sort of checking in a base ibis install with no backends required

nodes.title: Import large table from bigquery to duckdb
nodes.body:
Hi all,

I would like to read a large table from bigquery and write it to a local duckdb table, without materializing the entire thing in memory as an intermediate step. I can't directly pass the `ir.Table` to `duckdb_con.create_table`, it seems like it tries to execute the expression inside the duckdb context. Most examples I've seen call `to_pyarrow` on the table, but I assume that loads the entire table in memory. I also tried `to_pyarrow_batches()` and got

> Creating an `ibis.memtable` from a `pyarrow.RecordBatchReader` would load _all_ data into memory.

What is the right way to do it?

Thanks!

Related: https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/issues/11683, https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/issues/4800, https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/issues/8115.

I came up with the solution along these lines:

```python
t1 = ibis.examples.penguins.fetch()
t2 = con.create_table("penguins", schema=t1.schema(), overwrite=True)
for b in t1.to_pyarrow_batches(chunk_size=10):
    con.insert("penguins", b)
```

Is there a more convenient way to achieve it?

nodes.title: PyExasol 1.0.0
nodes.body:
In [Ibis](https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis), [its Exasol backend](https://ibis-project.org/backends/exasol) uses the function pyexasol.connect. Its usage of PyExasol is currently pinned to [pyexasol>=0.25.2"] (https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/commit/9eb90ace3969b026cae58ba8b974bb3814feb3ec) and does not have an upper bound. Today, we released PyExasol 1.0.0. This includes breaking changes to the function `pyexasol.connect`, where the goal of these changes is to improve data transfer security. For more details on the changes, please refer to the [PyExasol version 1.0.0 release notes](https://github.com/exasol/pyexasol/releases/tag/1.0.0).

In particular, updating to PyExasol version 1.0.0 may affect users using Ibis' backend connection to Exasol via `do_connect(self, user, password, host='localhost', port=8563, timezone='UTC', **kwargs)` (see [reference](https://ibis-project.org/backends/exasol#ibis.backends.exasol.Backend.do_connect)). websocket_sslopt=None is one of the default input values for the function pyexasol.connect(..) (see [reference](https://exasol.github.io/pyexasol/master/api.html#pyexasol.ExaConnection)), which is internally mapped to:

    {"cert_reqs": ssl.CERT_NONE} for PyExasol versions < 1.0.0 .
    {"cert_reqs": ssl.CERT_REQUIRED} for PyExasol version >=1.0.0.

If upgrading to PyExasol version 1.0.0 results in breaking changes, Ibis users should:
* Refer to the PyExasol's [Security page](https://exasol.github.io/pyexasol/master/user_guide/configuration/security.html) to determine which values are appropriate for their use case.
* Add their needed values into the **kwargs of `do_connect(...)`, which are later passed onto the function `pyexasol.connect(...)`.

nodes.title: Best way to query a table with a predefined macro in DuckDB
nodes.body:
Hello all,

I've decided that Ibis would be a great tool for me to work with DuckDB files. Currently, I produce a `.ddb` file and hand it off to another person to query.

An example dataset I have in this `.ddb` file I produce is a bunch of temperatures e.g.

```python
import ibis
import pandas as pd
data = pd.DataFrame({"temperature": [0,0,1,5,3], "count": [0,1,2,3,4]})
conn = ibis.duckdb.connect()
temperatures = conn.create_table("temperatures", data)
```

Since temperature values can exist in a bunch of tables, I want to use a macro to make it easier to query. It makes sense to me, given the nature of ibis, that there is no nice API to create it, so I resort to `raw_sql`:

```python
conn.raw_sql("CREATE OR REPLACE MACRO celsius_to_fahrenheit(temp) AS 32 + (temp * (9/5))")
```

However, I couldn't find a nice way for the end-user to query `temperatures` with my macro. The best I have is:

```python
conn.sql("SELECT celsius_to_fahrenheit(temperature) FROM temperatures").execute()
```

which to me, defeats the purpose of using Ibis. I would like for something slightly more developer-friendly, something akin to maybe:

```python
temperatures.select(celsius=temperatures.temperature, fahrenheit=temperatures.sql("celsius_to_farenheit(temperature)"))
```

but that gives me an exception. Is there any better way of utilizing it than using `connection.sql`?

nodes.title: Is it possible to create "placeholders" in an Ibis expression?

nodes.title: Mutating in a loop with `isin` using expressions as value doesn't work as expected
nodes.body:
Given a set of tables `a, b, ...` with the same column name `id`, my goal is to create a new table with a column `id` containing all possible `id` values and for each table a boolean column `in_a, in_b, ...` containing `true` if the specific table also has the specific `id` value. Sample code:

```python
import ibis
import polars as pl

u = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]})  # all possible ids
a = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
b = pl.DataFrame({"id": [2, 3]})

con = ibis.polars.connect({"u": u, "a": a, "b": b})

# desired output:
# id,   in_a,   in_b
# 1,    true,   false
# 2,    true,   true
# 3,    false,  true

u = con.table("u")
t_names = ["a", "b"]
tables = [con.table(t) for t in t_names]

for t, name in zip(tables, t_names):
    u = u.mutate(**{f"in_{name}": u["id"].isin(t["id"])})

print(u.to_polars())
# actual output:
# id,   in_a,   in_b
# 1,    true,   true
# 2,    true,   true
# 3,    true,   true
```

However, changing the argument to `isin` to be static, e.g.
```python
u = u.mutate(**{f"in_{name}": u["id"].isin(t["id"]).to_polars()})
```
gives the right answer. Wondering if this is expected behaviour or a bug?

I think I've narrowed down the issue to dynamic lookup using expressions inside `isin` not working on the `polars` backend. For the duckdb backend this works as expected:

```python
import ibis

u = ibis.memtable({"id": [1, 2, 3]})
a = ibis.memtable({"id": [1, 2]})
b = ibis.memtable({"id": [2, 3]})

tables = {"a": a, "b": b}
for name, t in tables.items():
    u = u.mutate(**{f"in_{name}": u["id"].isin(t["id"])})
print(u)
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ in_a    ┃ in_b    ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ boolean │ boolean │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│     1 │ True    │ False   │
│     2 │ True    │ True    │
│     3 │ False   │ True    │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘
```

But setting backed to `polars` results in the wrong answer:

```python
import ibis

ibis.set_backend("polars")

u = ibis.memtable({"id": [1, 2, 3]})
a = ibis.memtable({"id": [1, 2]})
b = ibis.memtable({"id": [2, 3]})

tables = {"a": a, "b": b}
for name, t in tables.items():
    u = u.mutate(**{f"in_{name}": u["id"].isin(t["id"])})
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ in_a    ┃ in_b    ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ boolean │ boolean │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│     1 │ True    │ True    │
│     2 │ True    │ True    │
│     3 │ True    │ True    │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘
```
How is this typically expressed in Polars?

The specific problem here is that polars doesn't appear to have a way to specify that two columns named "id" are coming from two different dataframes, whereas in DuckDB (and SQL in general) this is usually an `IN (<subquery>)`.

I suppose this could be done with a semi join, let me see if I can get that working.
Looks like `with_context` might be the way to do this.

Nope, that doesn't work (and it's deprecated).

It seems like this is basically ~impossible to do concisely and/or without resorting to hacks like materializing one or both sides of the computation.

We had this same exact problem in the pandas backend (which no longer exists in Ibis), and the workaround to handle this problem was truly awful: we ended up having to temporarily rename columns to something unique and then "unrename" them.

Maybe there was a better way to do it, but polars should really allow column disambiguation at the expression level, without requiring a lazyframe/dataframe object, or renaming to do so.

Even in the simplified example of just one `isin` lookup and static variables the ibis version doesn't work - I assume this is because polars is only seeing the first dataframe and not the second one:

```python
import ibis
import polars as pl

upl = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]})  # all posisble ids
apl = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})

u, a = ibis.memtable(upl), ibis.memtable(apl)

# pure polars
upl.with_columns(in_a=pl.col("id").is_in(apl["id"]))   # works although this is deprecated, encouraged to convert to list: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/22149
```
```
┌─────┬───────┐
│ id  ┆ in_a  │
│ --- ┆ ---   │
│ i64 ┆ bool  │
╞═════╪═══════╡
│ 1   ┆ true  │
│ 2   ┆ true  │
│ 3   ┆ false │
└─────┴───────┘
```
```python
# ibis
u.mutate(a_in=u["id"].isin(a["id"]))  # doesn't work
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ a_in    ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ boolean │
├───────┼─────────┤
│     1 │ True    │
│     2 │ True    │
│     3 │ True    │
└───────┴─────────┘
```

Now if we change the example so that the column in `apl/a` has a different name, then with ibis we get a `ColumnNotFoundError` since, I assume, polars is trying to find `id2` in `upl/u`:
```python
apl = apl.with_columns(id2=pl.col.id)
a = ibis.memtable(apl)
u.mutate(a_in=u["id"].isin(a["id2"]))
```
```
...
ColumnNotFoundError: id2

Resolved plan until failure:

        ---> FAILED HERE RESOLVING 'sink' <---
SELECT [col("id")]
  DF ["id"]; PROJECT */1 COLUMNS
```

The workaround with a join (+ mutate after) works:

```python
upl = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]})  # all posisble ids
apl = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
bpl = pl.DataFrame({"id": [2,3]})

u, a, b = ibis.memtable(upl), ibis.memtable(apl), ibis.memtable(bpl)
tables = {"a": a, "b": b}

for name, t in tables.items():
    u = u.join(t, u.id==t.id, how="left", rname=f"in_{name}").mutate(**{f"in_{name}": _[f"in_{name}"].notnull()})
u
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ in_a    ┃ in_b    ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ boolean │ boolean │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│     1 │ True    │ False   │
│     2 │ True    │ True    │
│     3 │ False   │ True    │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘
```
What is the non-deprecated, pure polars solution to this? We can try to use that inside Ibis.

I'm not sure there is one, reading https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/22149, the reason seems tangential, e.g. to disambiguate when looking up things in list rows. The warning given when using polars `is_in` looking up values in the series of another dataframe suggests to materialize the lookup values to a Python list. But anyway, in my example `upl.with_columns(in_a=pl.col("id").is_in(apl["id"]))`, the `apl["id"]` is not an expression but a materialized series already.

This thread might be relevant - the suggestions seem to range from using lazyframes to using joins instead of lookups which should be faster in any case: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/4670

Not entirely following why this is an anti pattern, but 🤷🏻.

If you're immediately using the boolean column as a filter, then yes, a semi or anti join is what you probably should be using, though most query engines recognize the pattern and convert it to one of those for you as part of query optimization.

If you need the boolean column for some non-filtration purpose, then it seems like your best bet is to use joins for now.

I tried an approach that gets this working, but it uses a combination of `map_batches` and materializing one side of the `is_in`, so it's pretty much a performance hellscape.

Hello,

I am having a problem with multiple backends.

`IbisError: Multiple backends found for this expression`
 
I am using a Snowflake as a backend. Source data is in one schema, and tables are written in another, which I will call the 'destination' schema. When using tables in the destination schema, i get the above error.

Is this a known/required behavior? Is it possible to select one of the backends? I am able to list the backends using `table._find_backends()` source code [here](https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/blob/d2f8839dc0e0d2202139aa66fc97194f630ffd18/ibis/expr/types/core.py#L289)

The analysis pipeline is quite complex and sometimes intermediate tables already written to SNOWFLAKE_DEST_DATABASE need to be joined on tables in the SNOWFLAKE_SOURCE_DATABASE.

con1 = ibis.snowflake.connect(

    warehouse=SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE,
    role=SNOWFLAKE_ROLE,

    account=SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT,
    warehouse=SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE,
    role=SNOWFLAKE_ROLE,

tbl1.join(tbl2, "PERSON_ID")
```

This code works. It's a little weird to me because the connector is initialized with the SOURCE database, but it works. 

Is this clearer what we're trying to do? Is the solution we came up with the recommended approach?

nodes.title: How do I create a udtf in snowflake?
nodes.body:
I'm looking for a new techstack to migratie from spark to snowflake. The options are
- snowpark
- ibis
- pandas on snowflake

Is it possible to create a udtf in ibis like in snowpark? https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark/python/creating-udtfs

### Quick Comparison

<html>
<body>
<!--StartFragment--><html><head></head><body>

Feature                                           | Snowpark (Python) | Ibis                                                  | Pandas on Snowflake

Native UDTF support                      | ✅ Full support      | ❌ Not supported (as of 2025)     | ❌ Not supported

Ease of deployment on Snowflake | ✅ Excellent           | ⚠️ Limited (depends on backend)| ✅ Excellent

Interoperability with Python           | ✅ Full Python integration | ✅ Good (but abstracted) | ✅ Pandas-like

Suitable for heavy logic                  | ✅ Ideal                 | ⚠️ Somewhat limited                     | ❌ Not meant for complex logic

Declarative API                               | ❌ Imperative        | ✅ Yes                                             | ✅ Yes

</body></html><!--EndFragment-->
</body>
</html>

### Why Snowpark is Necessary for UDTFs
Snowpark gives you access to the Snowflake Python API that integrates tightly with Snowflake's compute and allows defining UDFs, UDTFs, and stored procedures in Python, including:
```
python
@udtf(output_schema=["word", "length"])
class SplitWords:
    def process(self, text: str):
        for word in text.split():
            yield (word, len(word))
```
 
This kind of procedural, stateful control is currently not available in Ibis, which is focused on declarative query construction rather than function registration/execution.

### Recommendation
If UDTFs or UDFs are a critical part of your workload, Snowpark is the only viable option in this stack today. If you just need to write expressive SQL pipelines in Python, Ibis is great.

Hello,

LLMs generally have a lot of trouble producing valid Ibis code, particularly because (unlike packages like Pandas) its use is not widespread.

To overcome this, I was considering guiding the LLM by asking it to prioritize the use of the `con.sql` function, which allows it to perform certain processing operations directly in SQL (generally well-understood by the models) while retrieving Ibis objects after each call.

My experiments led me to two questions.

First, I would like to be sure I understand the "dialect" parameter. If, for example, I use the polars backend, and I use `con.sql(<SQL>, dialect='postgres')`, this allows the SQL to be expressed in Postgres, and to be "translated" internally into Polars for execution? If so, this would be ideal because LLMs are very familiar with the Postgres dialect. More generally, it would be enough to force the LLM to use the dialect it masters best (without even having to know the actual backend), and Ibis would take care of translating the requests to the target backend alone.

Second, when using `con.sql`, is there a way to save the resulting table in the backend context, based on the name given to the assigned variable? This would make it easy to chain calls using any previously constructed tables. Here's an example:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a4063848-7c6f-47e1-a376-fc243a40ea04)

Here's the code if needed.
```python

con = ibis.polars.connect(
    {
        'clients': pl.LazyFrame({
                    'id': [1, 2, 3],
                    'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],

nodes.title: How to LATERAL VIEW explode
nodes.body:
Hi there! I have seen discussions arround doing such things:

```
SELECT element
FROM t
LATERAL VIEW explode(elements) s AS element;
```

But couldn't find a proper example of how to do it... Do you guys have something?

This operation is spelled using `t.my_column.unnest()` or `t.unnest("my_column")`.

**TL; DR**: start with the first form, and consider the second form if you need to generate array element offsets.

Here's a description of the two forms:

1. The first form is a column operation, that transforms an array column into a column with the expression of array element type. So, if the column type before calling `unnest()` is `array<T>`, then the type after calling `unnest()` is `T`. Here's the API documentation for that one: https://ibis-project.org/reference/expression-collections.html#ibis.expr.types.arrays.ArrayValue.unnest
2. The second form is slightly more advanced and produces a **table** instead of a new column. It's a cross join with the original table + the unnested column. This second form should be used if you need to generate offsets for the elements in the unnested array column. Here's the API docs for this one: https://ibis-project.org/reference/expression-tables#ibis.expr.types.relations.Table.unnest
Thanks a lot!

nodes.title: How is the lifecycle of an ibis connection instance managed?
nodes.body:
We use Ibis quite intensively within a solution that we develop in my company, with a postgresql backend. In particular, we have embedded certain features in a module so that the connection to our database is transparent for developers.

We then use our module every time we need to communicate with our Database.

Sometimes, we encounter problems that are quite complicated to resolve:
[1] We use .cache method on a table under construction and then, later, it is no longer accessible by its instance: "ibis_cached_[...] does not exist".
[2] We push a table into our database via Ibis functions (create_table, insert etc.), but we have a message "[...] does not exist" when we try to read it a little later in the process.

Unfortunately, despite multiple attempts, I have never managed to reproduce one of these problems in a minimal example case. However, when the problem appears during the development of a module, it is always reproducible in this specific situation (I just can't reproduce it in isolation).

Since we often use ibis across several modules, I thought that this kind of problem could occur in the case where we do not rigorously use the same Ibis connection instance everywhere. 
Example: In a module A I create an Ibis connection, I cache a table during the execution of a function of the module; this cached table is transmitted to another module B (in which another Ibis connection has been created, therefore another instance), module B is unable to use the cached table because it does not exist for it. 
As a solution, I set up a singleton via the syntax that I found here https://stackoverflow.com/a/12305404):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/eca3001a-de15-4f9f-8a0c-68123f75913b)

Since then, the problem [1] has not reproduced. However, the problem [2] continues to appear in certain situations. Recently this happened :
- I push a table t with Ibis into a Database, I try to read the table from database later in the same process: Ibis tells me that the table does not exist.
- To get around this, I push the table t with Ibis, but instead of reading it from the database and produce a new instance, I choose to continue using the instance t: my database no longer responds, and I am forced to restart it.

All this is very obscure and I am aware that it will be complicated to give me any help without being able to provide a minimal reproducible example. However, do the behaviors I describe mean anything to you? Do you have a lead to explore? Do you perhaps have some information on the management of the lifecycle of connections via Ibis that could explain this? In particular, how is the cataloging of tables created/deleted during a process managed by Ibis, which could explain why it is sometimes unaware of the existence of tables/caches that it has created itself?

Thank you in advance, any help is welcome.

Regards,

Hi @augcollet !  

Your singleton approach will resolve the missing cached tables -- for a bit of background there, when you call `cache` we create a temporary table with the results of the cached expression, but we also attach a finalizer to it that cleans up the table when the session ends.  

Postgres' temporary tables are bound to a given Postgres session, so that's why you can't see them in a separate connection instance.  If you want tables to persist between sessions and between connections, you need to pass the expression to `create_table`.

We don't keep track of the (persistent / non-temp) tables that we create -- they're accessible via the `information_schema` -- we track the temp tables we create so we can clean them up (although with Postgres that's not strictly necessary, due to the above referenced session-related cleanup).

As for the table creation issue -- that's strange behavior and Postgres is (famously) quite robust -- are you inserting huge quantities of data into postgres?  

The more detail you can provide, the better chance we have of helping to diagnose the issue.

If I understand correctly, each time Ibis needs to read a table it consults the database catalog in real time, so there is no reason why the table is invisible to Ibis when it does indeed exist (visible from dbeaver).

nodes.title: Catalog creation - DuckDB
nodes.body:
Hi Team,

is there a way/workaround to create catalogs for DuckDB backend?
We noticed that, for `duckdb.Backend`, we have `create_database`, `create_table`, `create_view`. However, we do not see any support for creating catalogs. 

To give more context:
Here is our requirement or what we are trying to do:

We have two individual backends: Trino and DuckDB

Let’s assume we have a Trino executable/compatible SQL(following trino’s catalog/schema/tables structure) as below:
```
SELECT * FROM catalog_1.schema_1.table_1 
```
We would like to have the same SQL to be executed for DuckDB backend as well, given we have DuckDB setup. We are able to achieve this using the following code:
```
con_duckdb = ibis.duckdb.connect(“catalog_1.duckdb”)
# loading the data
test_data = con_duckdb.read_parquet(“data.parquet”)
# creating database in duckdb : similar to a trino structure
con_duckdb.create_database(“schema_1”)
# creating a table under catalog and database 
con_duckdb.create_table(name=“table_1”, obj=test_data, database=“catalog_1.schema_1”)
# above steps complete the DuckDB setup based on our Trino SQL

# running the Trino compatible SQL on DuckDB
con_duckdb.sql(“SELECT * FROM catalog_1.schema_1.table_1”)
```

However, there may be a case where we have multiple catalogs in the SQL query:
```
SELECT
  # select columns
  FROM catalog_1.schema_1.table_1 as one
    INNER JOIN catalog_2.schema_2.table_2 as two
  WHERE
    # where condition 
```
In order for us to use the above SQL on DuckDB, we need the support for creating catalogs in DuckDB.

Please feel free to suggest if there is any better/alternative way to achieve this. TIA!

DuckDB supports the notion of catalogs but you can't have multiple catalogs in a given DuckDB file -- each file (or resource) corresponds to an individual catalog.  

In DuckDB SQL you can do `ATTACH IF NOT EXISTS 'catalog_1.db' as catalog_1;` and that will create a new DuckDB file called `catalog_1.db` if it doesn't already exists and make it available under the `catalog_1` identifier.

We wouldn't expose this as `create_catalog` because the semantics are a bit different from other systems that support catalogs -- e.g. if you connect to `file1.db` as a session, and then `ATTACH IF NOT EXISTS `file2.db` as file2;`, that association only lasts as long as the current session, so you would have to re-run the `ATTACH` command the next time you wanted to run a query that relied on both of those catalogs being available.

We do have the `attach` method on the DuckDB backend, although I don't believe it exposes the `IF NOT EXISTS` functionality at the moment.

Reference docs are here: https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/attach.html

nodes.title: Using ibis as a query builder without a backend
nodes.body:
Hey ibis team, dlthub developer here! With some delay I'm currently working on integrating ibis into our new dataset access feature. My current prototype basically has some glue code that creates an ibis backend from connection credentials that we know anyway, and the user can then use that backend/connection to do regular ibis stuff. 

I was wondering however if it is at all possible to use ibis just as a query builder. By that I mean constructing a query (in the form of a sqlglot-ast or some kind of other sqlglot object) with ibis expressions and then getting the sql statement in the dialect of your choosing. From what I can tell from reading your code, you can only build expressions tied to a backend and part of building an expression is also that reflection of the actual materialized schema on the database is done. I am thinking more of the way sqlalchemy works where you can build a query and then execute it at the end. Currently it look like I'd have to build my own backend to be able to achieve this, is that correct?

Some pseudocode of what I want I'd like to do to make it a bit clearer:

```
db = query_builder_backed()
# the two lines below should build an expression without connection to any database
t = db.table("penguins")
t.group_by("species", "island").agg(count=t.count()).order_by("count")
# the line below should return a sql statement for postgres which I can then use for my own pg connection
t.to_sql(dialect="postgres")
```

Thanks for asking!

This is definitely a core use case of ibis, that is, using it to build expressions without a backend.

The primary way you do this is by constructing what are called _unbound tables_, using the `ibis.table` function.

You can then compile the expression using `ibis.to_sql`, passing the `dialect` argument to compile the expression to a different SQL dialect.

Usually most folks want to execute these expressions in some way, and the way to do that is with one of the `to_*` methods like `con.to_pandas`. This method accepts both unbound expressions **and** bound expressions. Similarly for `con.to_pyarrow`.

The primary thing you as the user needs to provide to `ibis.table` is the schema.

Hey @cpcloud! Thanks for the quick and comprehensive answer. That is indeed pretty nice and exactly what I need :) Out of curiousity I have one followup question: In the code base I saw quite a bit of code that seems to be specifically taylored to certain databases / datasources. Is this to support sql / expression features that are not supported natively by sqlglot?

Hey @sh-rp -- sometimes it's to support things that sqlglot doesn't explicitly support, but that are easy enough to spell. A lot of our backend-specific code is also aimed at trying to get consistent results, so standardizing on things like a 0-indexed day-of-week to match Python semantics
Alright thanks!

I have one additional question: Is there a way to select a default database (database as defined in the ibis world) for an ibis backend? Similar to how you can set the default schema on postgres with "SET search_path TO myschema;"? Or is it advisable to always provide the database name when listing and retrieving tables?

Hey @sh-rp -- setting the database you connect to can almost always be handled in the `connect` call.  So something like

```python
con = ibis.postgres.connect(..., database="default_database_when_listing")
```

For the local options like DuckDB, that's more a function of which duckdb file you pass to `connect`, but for the "traditional" remote engines, the way to specify the default is in the connection string.

Hey @gforsyth, thanks! I saw that but since it works a bit different for each connection and most table constructors take database as an argument, i thought maybe there would be a unified interface to set a database for an SQLBackend that then gets applied when getting or saving a table. But I think we will let the users to that for now.

Apart from that, if you're interested you can follow my integration work in these two approaches, which I hope will be on the devel branch of dlt in the foreseable future :)

Ibis integration 1:
These are basically some helpers to create an ibis backend from credentials already known from a dlt destination configuration: https://github.com/dlt-hub/dlt/pull/2004.

Ibis integration 2:
Here I am only using the query building part of Ibis to access what we call datasets (databases in your world + a known dlt schema with additional hints) but the actual execution of the query is done via our own dbapi cursor wrappers and arrow / pandas / python tuple iterators. This will probably support all of our sql based destinations except for dremio which does not seem to have a sqlglot dialect, but maybe another dialect will partly work for that: https://github.com/dlt-hub/dlt/pull/2046

I have another question about the Expressions. Given a couple of unbound tables with a schema I provided and one expression deriving from those tables, let's say a Join, a column subselection, a renaming of one columns and a limit, how can I trace which of the resulting columns came from which original table and column name? I saw that it probably is possible to traverse the Expression tree, but I have not found a fairly straightforward way to do this. Is this possible at the moment?

We have a collection of traversal utilities in `ibis.common.graph`. The main entry points are any public functions e.g., `traverse`, `bfs`, `dfs` and the `Graph` class.

Note that the module itself **is not public** and so its API cannot be relied upon for stability across major releases.

That said, the `ibis.common.graph` API almost never changes in practice.

@cpcloud, thanks for pointing me in this direction! I'll have to do a bit more digging on how to achieve what I need then :) If we use the graph helpers, we will surely have tests in place to be alerted if this stuff changes. You probably know this anyway, but ibis is a pretty awesome project I must say :)

Hi everybody. I've been tasked with syncing tables between BigQuery and our customers infrastructure. I create JSON representations of the customer data and then run a custom Python script with Ibis to ingest this into BigQuery. 

I'm having issues with Type inference. See the problem is that a table gets created on BigQuery through Ibis and it receives a particular schema that it infers from the content of the JSON I send it. The problem is that the customer data is sparse and it is not uncommon for a particular column to have NULL for every single value. 

This creates two challenges. 1. Correctly inferring the column type when you create the table and 2. Correctly matching the incoming data type to the already existing table when new data is coming in. 

Since you never know when an entire column could be NULL, it makes this difficult.

My current solution is to send a dummy row with every JSON request. This dummy row has fake data in it, but with the correct type. This is there to ensure that we correctly infer the type when we sync it to BigQuery. So if there's a key called "Name"
I'll populate it's value with the word "STRING" in big capital letters in this dummy row to ensure there's at least one row with a value in it to help type inference down the line. 

At this point it is useful to show you some of my code:
``` python  
    print(f"Request Received | dataset_id: {dataset_id} | table_name: {table_name}")
    con = ibis.bigquery.connect(
        project_id=project_id,
        dataset_id=dataset_id,
        credentials=credentials
    )

    # Load CSV into a DataFrame
    df = pd.read_json(StringIO(json_data))
    df = df.infer_objects()

    #Append a new column and mark the last entry (which should be a dummy row) for deletion
    df["deletionFlag"] = False
    df.loc[df.index[-1],'deletionFlag'] = True

    #Prepare SQL to clear the dummy row we use for type inference
    sql = f"DELETE FROM `{project_id}.{dataset_id}.{table_name}` WHERE deletionFlag = TRUE;"

    # Check if the table already exists
    table_exists = table_name in con.list_tables()

    if table_exists:
        # Fetch the schema of the existing table
        client = bq.Client(credentials=credentials, project=project_id)
        table_ref = client.dataset(dataset_id).table(table_name)
        table = client.get_table(table_ref)
        existing_schema = {field.name: field.field_type for field in table.schema}
        print(f"Table exists | Schema: {existing_schema}")

        # Convert DataFrame to match the schema
        for column, dtype in existing_schema.items():
            if column in df.columns:
                if dtype == 'STRING':
                    df[column] = df[column].astype(str)
                elif dtype == 'INTEGER':
                    df[column] = pd.to_numeric(df[column], errors='coerce').fillna(0).astype(int)
                elif dtype == 'FLOAT':
                    df[column] = pd.to_numeric(df[column], errors='coerce').fillna(0.0).astype(float)

Schematically, the resulting query would have been constructed like this:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6669d808-cc5b-4df6-9c6f-bd7239cd5bc4)

nodes.title: Define schemas with pydantic
nodes.body: Is there a way to define table schemas as pydantic models and use that as the source of truth for what the data contains, irrespective of the backend used (duckdb in my case)?

Hey @tgy!

We don't have explicit support for `pydantic` models, but you can create table definitions irrespective of data in a backend (or, in fact, without ever using or connecting to a backend).  We call these `UnboundTable`s:

```python

>>> import ibis

>>> sch = ibis.schema({"a": "array<int>", "b": "float32", "c": "str"})

>>> ibis.table(sch, name="my_table")
UnboundTable: my_table
  a array<int64>
  b float32
  c string
```

Or if you prefer to not use our string-parsing to get the datatypes, you can use explicit ibis dtypes:

```python
>>> import ibis.expr.datatypes as dt

>>> sch = ibis.schema({"a": dt.Array(dt.int), "b": dt.float32, "c": dt.str})

>>> ibis.table(sch, name="my_table")
UnboundTable: my_table
  a array<int64>
  b float32
  c string
```

Alternatively, if you have a schema-like thing defined in any one of `numpy`, `pandas`, `polars`, or `pyarrow`, you can do:

```python

>>> from ibis.expr.schema import Schema

>>> sch = Schema.from_polars(schema_obj)  # or `pyarrow`, etc...
```


Now you can operate on this table like any other table

```python
>>> t = ibis.table(sch, name="my_table")

>>> expr = t.mutate(c=t.c.replace("foo", "bar"))

>>> expr
r0 := UnboundTable: my_table
  a array<int64>
  b float32
  c string

Project[r0]
  a: r0.a
  b: r0.b
  c: StringReplace(r0.c, pattern='foo', replacement='bar')
```

Once you have the expression how you want it (or just to test it out) you can run it against actual data by doing something like

```python

con = ibis.duckdb.connect("my_db_with_that_actual_table_definition.ddb")

con.to_pandas(expr)
```

It's nice to define a schema for the table, but I would like the types of my objects to be defined in a single place, and this definition is used both at the Python-level (single object or list of objects being manipulated) and at the ibis(table)-level.

```python

>>> import ibis.expr.datatypes as dt

>>> @dataclass
      ...: class MyTable:
      ...:     a: dt.int32
      ...:     b: dt.str

    list_tables = glob("/lakehouse/default/Tables/*/*/", recursive=True)

attach_lakehouse(ws,catalog)

my problem is, I don't know how to tell ibis to create those tables in the database db, currently it goes to main by default ?

What is `catalog` for you in the call `attach_lakehouse(ws,catalog)`?
in onelake, we have three naming convention, catalog, database then table

see more details, I want the table to be under dbo and ny not main , notice, catalog and database works as expected, the only issue is how to create the table under the correct location, catalog.database

When you use any `read_*` method, it isn't going to create a persistent table (this is true across all backends) -- it either creates a temporary table or a temporary view (for DuckDB, it's a temp view).

The view is going to be created in the database `main` -- we could probably add an option to target where the view is created, but to _persist_ the table elsewhere, you can pass the `view` object to `create_table` and specify which database you want to persist the table in, e.g.

```python

>>> con = ibis.duckdb.connect()

>>> con.list_databases()
['information_schema', 'main', 'pg_catalog']

>>> con.create_database("new")

>>> con.list_databases()

>>> # now persist that data to a table in a different `database`

>>> con.create_table("awards", t, database="new")
DatabaseTable: memory.new.awards
  playerID string
  awardID  string
  yearID   int64
  lgID     string
  tie      string
  notes    string

>>> con.list_tables(database="new")
['awards']
```
I see, thanks, but i don't want to persist the data, I want to keep it as a view

You can use 
```
con.create_view("awards", t, database="new")
```

it'll still show in `con.list_tables(database="new")` because at the moment it list everything, tables and views. There is a PR in the works to separate the listing of views vs tables though.
thanks, that works !!!

nodes.title: Farewell pandas, and thanks for all the fish. – Ibis
nodes.body:
# Farewell pandas, and thanks for all the fish. – Ibis

the portable Python dataframe library

https://ibis-project.org/posts/farewell-pandas/

<!-- sha1: 763130825f31fdd0b3d06b879c385f5fea439916 -->
Without pandas and dask, which backends are left that aren't SQL based?  Are you aiming to stop supporting non-sql backends in general?

It will only be the `polars` backend that isn't SQL based, and once their SQL support is at feature-parity, we'll probably move to using SQL there, too.  We aren't aiming to stop supporting non-SQL backends, though -- if there's a deferred query engine we're happy to wire it up.

And while it was a joke, Phillip Cloud's `ibish` is a pretty great demonstration that the Ibis IR is flexible enough to talk to just about _anything_: https://ibis-project.org/posts/unix-backend/

It is somewhat bittersweet for me to see the pandas backend go since I've rewritten it from the ground up a couple months ago https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/pull/7797 vastly simplifying it, improving its memory management and operation support, it was still a burden that we had to handle in order to ship ibis' internal refactors. 

The main point where the ibis backend stands out of the rest, is that ibis actually implements an execution engine on top of pandas functions as compute kernels. Although both the dask and polars backends use the rewrite rules from the pandas backend to transform the logical plan to a dataframe API compatible flavor, they don't need to implement an execution engine, just building up a lazy execution plan of that particular backend.
I certainly hope that `daft` will replace `dask` at some point in the future.
For folks interested in the progress here's the issue on `daft` support as a backend: https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/issues/8904

With pandas backend gone, will that impact export functionality like `.to_pandas()`? I see a lot of value in keeping at least this functionality around to allow users to perform downstream tasks and interface with dataframe libraries that were designed around pandas (Seaborn, Bokeh, Plotly, etc.).

Pandas will remain around as an input and output type of ibis. You can still pass pandas dataframes to `create_table` or `memtable`, and you can still get results in pandas with `to_pandas`. The only thing that's going away is using pandas as the backing compute engine (the `ibis.pandas` backend).
As a contributor who has had to add/modify pandas special cased stuff when submitting a PR, I am excited that this cruft is getting removed.

nodes.title: How can I check if an array field contains a certain value OR the array field is null?
nodes.body:
I have a set of documents. Some documents are versioned; others are not. A single document can belong to multiple versions.

In my document database, relevant versions are stored in a JSON field. For example,

```python
import ibis

ibis.options.interactive = True

ddb = ibis.duckdb.connect("mydb.duckdb")

schema = ibis.schema(
    {
        "id": "int64",
        "json_data": "json",
    }
)

ddb.drop_table("mytable", force=True)
ddb.create_table("mytable", schema=schema)

data = [
    {"id": 1, "json_data": {"versions": ["v1", "v2"]}},
    {"id": 2, "json_data": {"versions": ["v3"]}},
    {"id": 3, "json_data": {}},
]

ddb.insert("mytable", data)

t = ddb.table("mytable")

t.select(
    t.id,
    t.json_data["versions"],
)
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ JSONGetItem(json_data, 'versions') ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ json                               │
├───────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│     1 │ ['v1', 'v2']                       │
│     2 │ ['v3']                             │
│     3 │ NULL                               │
└───────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

I can filter for documents where `version` contains `v2` or `v3`:

```python
t.filter(
    t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v2")
    | t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v3")
)
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ json_data           ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ json                │
├───────┼─────────────────────┤
│     1 │ {'versions': [...]} │
│     2 │ {'versions': [...]} │
└───────┴─────────────────────┘```

```

and I can filter for documents that are "unversioned" (thus being relevant to all versions):

```python
t.filter(
    t.json_data["versions"] == None
)
```
```
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ id    ┃ json_data          ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ int64 │ json               │
├───────┼────────────────────┤
│     3 │ {'versions': None} │
└───────┴────────────────────┘
```

But how do I get all documents that are relevant to a specific version, *or* are unversioned (and thus still relevant)?

```python
t.filter(
    t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1")
    | t.json_data["versions"] == None
)
```
```
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[71], [line 2](vscode-notebook-cell:?execution_count=71&line=2)
      [1](vscode-notebook-cell:?execution_count=71&line=1) t.filter(
----> [2](vscode-notebook-cell:?execution_count=71&line=2)     t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1")
      [3](vscode-notebook-cell:?execution_count=71&line=3)     | t.json_data["versions"] == None
      [4](vscode-notebook-cell:?execution_count=71&line=4) )

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'BooleanColumn' and 'JSONColumn'
```

(And, am I thinking about method chaining in the right way for JSON-based arrays, or am I missing some fundamentally better approach?)

Thanks in advance!

You're missing the `()` around the `t.json_data["versions"] == None`.

The `|` operator binds tighter than `==`, so the parentheiszation (the way the Python interpreter sees it) of what you've written is actually

```python
(t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1") | t.json_data["versions"]) == None
```

You'll need to parenthesize any binary operators in the specific way that you want to evaluate them when any of the bitwise operators (`|`, `&`, and `^`) are in an expression.

In this case that'd be:

```python
t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1") | (t.json_data["versions"] == None)
```

Running that in IPython:

```
In [14]: t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1") | (t.json_data["versions"] == None)
Out[14]:
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Or(ArrayContains(Cast(JSONGetItem(json_data, 'versions'), array<string>), 'v1'), IsNull(JSONGetItem(json_data, 'versions'))) ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ boolean                                                                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                                                                                         │
│ False                                                                                                                        │
│ True                                                                                                                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Alternatively, you can use the `isnull()` method, which wouldn't require parentheses because there are binary operators involved in using it.

```python
t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1") | t.json_data["versions"].isnull()
```

This is:

1. Not something Ibis can do anything about, it's part of the Python grammar and therefore baked into the language.
2. Unfortunately a common pitfall for folks who've not yet had to deal with it, and/or are coming from other data analysis platforms like MATLAB and R where `==` operator binds tighter than the the `|` operator.

A complete and clear answer - thank you! I was too distracted with thinking about methods to also consider the usual expression evaluation stuff. Now it makes sense.

A follow-up question - logical Boolean operators have a lower precedence than comparison operators, but they don't seem to be supported:

```python
t.filter(
    (t.json_data["versions"].cast("array<str>").contains("v1"))
    or
    (t.json_data["versions"] == None)
)
```
```
...trace omitted...
ValueError: The truth value of an Ibis expression is not defined
```

I don't see an enhancement issue filed for this. Is this a reasonable request to file, or is it not already implemented for logistical reasons?
Python itself doesn't allow overloading `or`, `and`, or `not`, so the best we can do is to overload `|`, `&`, and `~`.

```sql
SELECT
  *
FROM
  `bigquery-public-data.pypi.file_downloads`
WHERE
  project = 'kedro'
  AND TIMESTAMP("${runtime_params:start_date, ${globals:start_date}}") <= timestamp
  AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP("${runtime_params:end_date, ${globals:end_date}}")

        ibis.timestamp("2024-07-01") <= pypi_kedro_raw_lazy.timestamp,

which returns:

SELECT
  *
FROM `bigquery-public-data`.`pypi`.`file_downloads` AS `t0`
WHERE
  `t0`.`project` = 'kedro'
  AND DATETIME('2024-07-01T00:00:00') <= `t0`.`timestamp`
  AND `t0`.`timestamp` < DATETIME('2024-07-02T00:00:00')
LIMIT 5

Hi @astrojuanlu -- get ready for a feeling of deep dread.

In BigQuery, `DATETIME`s have no time zone, `TIMESTAMP`s have a time zone.
If you use `ibis.timestamp` and don't specify a time zone, when it compiles to BigQuery, will give you a `DATETIME`.

    ...:         pypi_kedro_raw_lazy.timestamp < ibis.timestamp("2024-07-02", timezone="UTC"),
    ...:     ])
    ...:     .head(5)
    ...: ))
SELECT
  *
FROM `bigquery-public-data`.`pypi`.`file_downloads` AS `t0`
WHERE
  `t0`.`project` = 'kedro'

```

nodes.title: Is there a way to extract the DDL generated by the `create_table` method?
nodes.body:
I would like to manipulate some of the data types that `ibis` is deciding for some of the fields of a table which I intend to create on a given backend e.g. doing the below
```python
import ibis

t = ibis.memtable({"a": [1.0,2,3], "b": ["x", "y", "zz"]})

conn = ibis.mssql.connect()

ddl_sql = t.schema().to_sql(
    # dialect = "mssql",  #  either this or the backend as another argument
    conn
)
print(ddl_sql)
```
could give me
```sql
CREATE TABLE [dbo].[<some name>]
(
	[a] [bigint]  NULL,
	[b] [varchar(max)]  NULL -- this is the one I would like to change to, let's say, `varchar(2)`
)
```
and then maybe use `ibis.raw_sql` as mentioned in this [thread](https://github.com/ibis-project/ibis/discussions/7358#discussioncomment-7277328)

I know, a method like this does not exist in the current version of `ibis` but is there any workaround because I know `ibis` _would_ generate the DDL when the `conn.create_table` method would be called.

I think we could probably add a `.compile()` method to our `Schema` object, which would get you everything between the parentheses and would probably clean up a bunch of our internals in the various `create_table` methods.

For example, we could likely easily get you the `expressions` list here:

```
In [1]: import sqlglot as sg

In [2]: sg.parse_one("create table t (x int, y int)")
Out[2]:
Create(
  this=Schema(
    this=Table(
      this=Identifier(this=t, quoted=False)),
    expressions=[
      ColumnDef(
        this=Identifier(this=x, quoted=False),
        kind=DataType(this=Type.INT, nested=False)),
      ColumnDef(
        this=Identifier(this=y, quoted=False),
        kind=DataType(this=Type.INT, nested=False))]),
  kind=TABLE)
```
ok this would be great !

Also I asked this because as long as #9382 is not solved, I am trying to workaround it. I won't need to go this way if we could simply have something like
```python
t = t.mutate(
    some_string_column = t['some_string_column'].cast(ibis.dtype('string(2)')) # which can get translated to `VARCHAR(2)` in the DDL query used by `create_table`
)
```
Ok, well funny enough I put up a draft PR for that earlier this morning 😄
